[[File:1st order Griewank function.png|thumb|200px|2D Plot of the one dimensional Griewank function]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Griewank [[Test functions for optimization|test function]]''' is a [[Smoothness|smooth]] multidimensional mathematical function used in unconstrained [[mathematical optimization|optimization]]. It is commonly employed to evaluate the performance of [[global optimization]] algorithms. The function is defined as<ref>{{cite journal |last=Griewank |first=A. O. |title=Generalized descent for global optimization |journal=Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=11–39 |year=1981 |doi=10.1007/BF00933356}}</ref>

:<math>f(x) = 1 + \frac{1}{4000}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - \prod_{i=1}^n P_i(x_i),</math>

where <math>x = (x_1,\dots,x_n) \in \R^n</math> and <math>P_i(x_i)=\cos(x_i/\sqrt{i})</math>. The non-linear and [[convex function|non-convex]] function is characterized by its unique multimodal structure, featuring multiple local [[maximum and minimum|minima and maxima]] around its single global minimum at <math>x^\ast = 0</math>, where the function has minimal value <math>f(x^\ast) = 0</math>. The number of stationary points increases as the dimensionality <math>n</math> grows.

[[File:Griewank function 3D plot.png|thumb|200px|3D plot of the two dimensional Griewank function]]

For instance, the one-dimensional Griewank function <math>f(x_1) = 1+(1/4000)\cdot x_1^2-\cos(x_1)</math>
has 6365 [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical points]] in the interval <math>[-10000,10000]</math>, where the first derivative vanishes. These points satisfy the equation

:<math>\nabla f(x_1) = \frac{1}{2000} \cdot x_1 + \sin(x_1) = 0</math>.

[[File:2nd order Griewank function contour plot.png|thumb|200px|Contour plot of the two dimensional Griewank function]]

The multimodal structure of the Griewank function presents a challenge for many [[Deterministic algorithm|deterministic]] optimization algorithms, which may become trapped in one of the numerous local minima. This is particularly problematic for [[gradient]]-based methods. The Griewank function is commonly used to benchmark global optimization algorithms, such as [[genetic algorithms]] or [[particle swarm optimization]]. In addition to the original version, there are several variants of the Griewank function specifically designed to test algorithms in high-dimensional optimization scenarios.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Locatelli |first=M. |title=A note on the Griewank test function |journal=Journal of Global Optimization |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=169–174 |year=2003 |doi=10.1023/A:1021956306041}}</ref>

== Non-smooth variant ==

A non-smooth version of the Griewank function has been developed to emulate the characteristics of objective functions frequently encountered in optimization problems from [[machine learning]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bosse |first1=Torsten F. |last2=Bücker |first2=H. Martin |year=2026 |title=A piecewise smooth version of the Griewank function |journal=Optimization Methods and Software |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=347–357 |doi=10.1080/10556788.2024.2414186}}</ref> These functions often exhibit [[piecewise function|piecewise]] smooth or non-smooth behavior due to the presence of [[Regularization (mathematics)|regularization terms]], [[Activation function|activation functions]], or constraints in learning models.

A non-smooth variant of the Griewank function is the following:

: <math>
f(x) = 1 + \frac{1}{4000} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - \prod_{i=1}^n P_i(x_i) \text{ with } P_i(x_i)=\left| \cos\left(\frac{x_i}{2\sqrt{i}}\right) \right| - \left| \sin\left(\frac{x_i}{2\sqrt{i}}\right) \right|.
</math>

By incorporating non-smooth elements, such as absolute values in the cosine and sine terms, this function mimics the irregularities present in many ML loss landscapes. It offers a robust benchmark for evaluating optimization algorithms, especially those designed to handle the challenges of non-convex, non-smooth, or high-dimensional problems, including sub-gradient, hybrid, and evolutionary methods.

The function's resemblance to practical ML objective functions makes it particularly valuable for testing the robustness and efficiency of algorithms in tasks such as [[hyperparameter tuning]], neural network training, and constrained optimization.
